The carillon is a tuned percussion instrument of at least twenty-three bronze bells, hung fixed and tuned to the chromatic scale. The player strikes wooden keys with both hands and presses pedals with the feet, and steel wires and hammers strike the inner wall of the bells to make the sound. Its sounding class is Hornbostel–Sachs 111.242.222, the set of bells with internal strikers. Carillons usually stand in bell towers and are mostly owned by churches, universities or municipal bodies, and can also strike the hours or play short melodies by an automatic mechanism.

European automatic systems often use a playing drum to strike set tunes such as the Westminster quarters, while North America uses the playing drum less and rings the bells with pneumatic systems instead. 鐘琴起源可追溯至十六世紀低地國家（今比利時、荷蘭與法國低地地區）。一六四四年，J: The carillon's origins go back to the sixteenth-century Low Countries (present-day Belgium, the Netherlands and the lowlands of France). In 1644 Jacob van Eyck and the Hemony brothers cast the first tuned carillon, establishing the modern form. It peaked at the end of the eighteenth century, declined during the French Revolution, revived at the end of the nineteenth century, declined again during the First and Second World Wars, and revived once more after the war. UNESCO lists fifty-six belfries in Belgium and France as World Heritage and recognises Belgian carillon culture as intangible cultural heritage. About seven hundred survive, mostly in the Low Countries, with nearly two hundred in North America, almost all built in the twentieth century.
